intent: Wait for the third occurrence of a duplicated shape before extracting an abstraction, because two examples cannot distinguish the stable part from the coincidental part.
problem: An abstraction built at the second duplicate — or from a single example plus a forecast — encodes the two cases' accidental similarities, so the third case, which is where the real shape appears, forces a rewrite of the abstraction and every existing caller.
context: Applies whenever code, test or design shape repeats and someone is tempted to generalise it. It is a heuristic about the cost of a wrong abstraction, not a licence to leave duplication forever: after the third occurrence, extraction is the default, and after several more, a redesign may be cheaper than another extension. Two examples are the most data you can have and still not be able to tell a stable axis from an incidental one.
benefits: The abstraction that eventually appears is derived from three real cases, so its axis is the stable one.
Avoids the churn of building, then rebuilding, a general mechanism plus its callers.
Keeps early code direct; nothing pays indirection cost before it pays off.
Makes the third occurrence an explicit design checkpoint — a deliberate decision rather than an accident.
Works with, not against, YAGNI: the rule is "pay attention at two, abstract at three".
tradeoffs: Duplication exists until the third occurrence, and someone must remember to revisit it.
If the two early cases were already the wrong shape, extraction at three bakes in the wrong axis anyway.
Very rare, genuinely-coincident duplication is sometimes left in place, which reviewers read as sloppiness.
Hard to apply to code that is generated or copied wholesale — the count is not always visible.
Fighting the rule ("extract at two") is sometimes correct, and then the heuristic is wrong.
quality_attributes_note: simplicity 8 because the rule suppresses premature abstraction; extensibility 8 because the abstraction it eventually produces is the right one.

participants.responsibility: Build it directly; do not generalise.
participants.notes: Fowler's phrasing: the first time you do something, you just do it.
Note what differs between the two; the differences are the data you are collecting.
Now the commonality is evidenced rather than assumed.

use_cases: Leaving two near-identical validation functions until a third appears, then extracting one validator.
Writing the first two cases of a state machine inline before committing to a state pattern.
Repeating the same if-then chain twice, then noticing on the third that it is a lookup table.
Repeating a test setup twice, then extracting a fixture or builder on the third.
Building two adapters by hand before deciding the interface they imply.
avoid_when: The duplication is textual and identical (a shared constant, a schema) — extract immediately; the rule is about abstraction, not about duplication.
The second case already proves the axis will not hold (e.g. it needs a different shape entirely).
A security-critical or compliance artifact must be consistent across all copies.
The cost of the second copy is high in a way you can already measure (a 500-line migration script).
The extraction is a pure data one (a table of constants), not an abstraction choice.
pitfalls: Using the rule to justify leaving three, four, five copies — the rule ends at three.
Treating "three" as a magic number rather than as evidence that the abstraction is evidenced.
Forgetting to revisit at the third occurrence, so the duplication silently becomes the design.
Applying the rule to test data, where three similar tests may be testing three different things.
Extracting at three but choosing the axis from the first two cases out of habit.

related_patterns_notes.dry-principle: DRY says 'say it once'; Rule of Three says 'not yet, until the third' — they are read together, never separately.
related_patterns_notes.collecting-parameter: A repeated parameter list is the most common shape the rule tells you to wait on before building the Parameter Object.
related_patterns_notes.template-method: Two similar procedures with a differing step are the classic trigger for extracting a Template Method at the third.

anti_patterns: A generic base class named after a shape that only one subclass exhibits.
A configuration-driven engine parameterised for cases that do not exist.
Leaving four copies on the grounds that "the rule says three".
Extracting at the second occurrence and then reworking the abstraction when the third arrives.
design_principles: The first time you do something, you just do it. The second time you do something similar, you wince at the duplication, but you do the duplicate thing anyway. The third time you do something similar, you refactor (Don Roberts, via Martin Fowler, Refactoring, 2nd ed.).
Attempting premature refactoring risks selecting a wrong abstraction, which can result in worse code as new requirements emerge (after Sandi Metz, 'The Wrong Abstraction').
Prefer duplication over a wrong abstraction.
best_practices: Write a short comment at the second occurrence pointing at the third as the extraction point.
Diff the two copies when the third appears and extract only what is identical, not what is merely similar.
Track repetitions in review; a new third copy is the signal to stop and refactor.
Apply the rule to design shapes (state machines, strategies) as well as to code.
Let the rule expire: after the third, extraction is the default again.
sources: Martin Fowler, Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code, 2nd ed., Addison-Wesley 2018 (Don Roberts's guideline) — https://martinfowler.com/books/refactoring.html
Derick Bailey, Abstraction: The Rule Of Three, Los Techies, 2012 — https://lostechies.com/derickbailey/2012/10/31/abstraction-the-rule-of-three
Sandi Metz, The Wrong Abstraction, 2016 (cited as the cost of premature refactoring)
Don't make Clean Code harder to maintain, use the Rule of Three — https://understandlegacycode.com/blog/refactoring-rule-of-three
